The factual matrix of the case are as follows:-
The complainant is working as Project Manager for Cisco Systems, a Multi National Company.

The accused who claims to be conducting the business in real estate was introduced to the complainant through a common friend around three to four years ago and since getting in touch with the complainant the accused developed friendly ties and thus the complainant got closely acquainted with the accused person.

The accused person came to the residence of the complainant (Maruthi Layout,
Maragondanahalli, C.C.NO.52035/2023 Bangalore) and profusely requested for financial help of Rs.10,00,000/- (Rupees Ten lakhs only).

The accused disclosed that his property bearing No.8 situated at Muneshwara Temple street cross, Adugodi,
Bangalore, bearing PID No.67-28-8, was given as collateral security to Bank of India,
Bangalore, Main Branch, K.G. Road, Bangalore, while availing a loan and presently the said loan was declared NPA by the bank for non-payment and the said property was about to be subjected to be secured/taken over by the bank.

The accused profusely requested for financial help from the complainant and further told the complainant that he intends to get the said property released from the bank and sell it to prospective buyers immediately for a valuable sale consideration as otherwise the bank would adjust the property for the pending dues and the accused would suffer great loss.
The accused further assured the complainant that he would add interest at bank rates to Rs.10,00,000/- (i.e., loan amount sought) while returning back the C.C.NO.52035/2023 same.

The complainant who being very closely acquainted to the accused and on being profusely requested told the accused that he would help him with a handloan of Rs.10,00,000/- and thus the complainant agreed to transfer an amount of Rs.10,00,000/- to the recovery account of Bank of India (pertaining to the loan availed by the accused's family member from Bank of India).

On 03.10.2018 the complainant along with the accused met the bank officials of Bank of India, Main Branch, K.G. Road, Bangalore, and there the bank officials told that the amount could be transferred to 'Recovery under compromise' account No.84000SUNCR030 and the following day i.e., on 04.10.2018, the complainant transferred from his account at HDFC Bank, Kalkere Branch, Bangalore, an amount of Rs.10,00,000/- (Rupees Ten lakhs only) vide. RTGS to the 'Recovery under compromise' account No.84000SUNCR030.

The accused was aware that the mother of the complainant had a landed property at Muthagadahalli C.C.NO.52035/2023 village, Hesarghatta Hobli, Bangalore North Taluk, and accused suggested to the parents of the complainant that a shed could be constructed and let out on rent for some factory, so that the family could get some rental income, instead of keeping the land vacant.
The accused himself suggested that he was close to the few fabricators and they would take up the construction of the shed.
Thereafter, the accused brought one person by name Mujeeb and introduced him as a fabricator and it was decided that a shed be built at the cost of Rs.11,00,000/-.

The mother of the complainant executed an agreement dated 29.10.2018 with the said Mujeeb and it was decided that all the payments in stages should be made to the accused who in turn will hand it over to Mujeeb to facilitate construction of shed.

It is relevant to mention here that the complainant has adduced secondary evidence of the cheque in question as per the orders passed by this court on 06.04.2022 and it is marked as Ex.P14.

It is C.C.NO.52035/2023 relevant to mention here that the accused is not disputing the fact that Ex.P14 pertains to his account and he is also not disputing the fact that the signature on the said cheque in question belongs to him.

Such being the case, once the accused accepts and admits that the cheque in question pertains to the account of the accused and that the signature on the cheque in question pertains to him, the initial presumption as contemplated U/S 139 of the N.I Act has to be raised by the court in favour of the complainant, however, the accused is entitled to rebut the said presumption as held in the case of Sri Rangappa Vs. Sri Mohan by the Hon'ble Supreme Court reported in AIR 2010 SC 1898.
11.
Once the presumption U/S 139 and 118 of the Negotiable Instruments Act is raised, it is for the accused to rebut the said presumptions by adducing cogent evidence in support of his defence.

It is relevant to mention here that it is the specific defence of the accused taken in his reply notice at Ex.P12 C.C.NO.52035/2023 given in response to legal notice at Ex.P3 that there was an oral agreement between the complainant and the accused in relation to putting up construction measuring 4599 sq.ft. and compound wall measuring 3500 sq.ft. for Rs.26,00,000/- and the property belongs to the complainant situated near Yelahanka, Mukthakadahalli village, Shivakote,

On the other hand, the complainant has categorically stated in his complaint, in his chief-examination and also during his cross-examination that the amount of Rs.10,00,000/- was transferred by him to the recovery under compromise account of Bank of India as the accused approached the complainant saying that his above said property bearing No.8 situated at Muneshwara temple street cross, Adugodi, Bangalore,
which was given as collateral security to Bank of India had become N.P.A. and was subjected to be secured/taken over by the bank for non payment of the loan raised against it.

Further the Bank statement of the complainant which is produced at Ex.P7 pertaining to H.D.F.C., Bank clearly goes to show that on 04.10.2018 an amount of Rs.10,00,000/- has been C.C.NO.52035/2023 transferred to recovery under compromise account and the said entry clearly tallies with the claim of the complainant made in his complaint and falsifies the defence of the accused that the said money was transferred to the account of the accused towards construction of the shed agreed to be put up.

Further the bank statement produced by the complainant clearly reflects the entries relating to the amounts of Rs.30,000/-, Rs.10,000/-, Rs.2,000/-, Rs.2,00,000/- and Rs.1,00,000/- transferred to the account of the accused on 29.10.2018, 30.10.2018, 28.12.2018, 02.01.2019 and 02.01.2019 respectively.

It is the case of the complainant that the cheque in question was issued by the accused towards full and final settlement of repayment of above said amounts totally to the tune of Rs.13,42,000/- which he had agreed to repay it with bank rate of interest.

Further the accused during the cross-examination of PW1 though taken a defence that the amount shown to have been transferred to the accused as per Ex.P7 were paid for C.C.NO.52035/2023 the construction of the shed, PW1 has categorically denied it and inspite of it, the accused failed to adduce any cogent evidence in that respect.

Further the document at Ex.P13 which is said to be the receipt said to have been issued by the accused in favour of the complainant also falsifies the defence of the accused that the cost of the shed agreed to be put up was Rs.26,00,000/- and supports the case of the complainant that it was Rs.11,00,000/- and that towards the said money the accused had received advance of Rs.25,000/-.
Further the accused even has not denied the execution of the said receipt during the entire cross-examination of PW1.
Further the accused has failed to elicit from the mouth of PW1 in support of his defence during the entire cross- examination of PW1.

Further the police complaint said to have been lodged by the complainant which is at Ex.P9 also supports the case of the complainant regarding the accused receiving the money to the tune of Rs.13,42,000/- as loan as the said complaint has C.C.NO.52035/2023 been lodged by the complainant as a prudent man immediately two days later from the accused stealing the cheque and running away from the house of the complainant on 10.01.2020 as alleged in the compliant.

Further as could be seen from Ex.P11,
the complainant has also filed a private complaint against the accused for commission of the offence punishable under Section 420 and 506 of Indian Penal Code in relation to the facts which are averred in this complaint on 03.02.2020 as the written complaint given by the complainant to the Avalalli Police Station was not accepted on the evening of 10.01.2020 and after learning from the jurisdictional Police Station that they would treat it as N.C.R. by obtaining the statement of the accused.

It is relevant to mention here that merely denying the allegations of the complaint is not suffice to say that the accused either the accused has rebutted the presumptions available in favour of the complainant or raised any probable defence in view of my above discussion.

Further the complainant has done and taken all the necessary actions against the accused as a prudent man would have been done in the above said facts and circumstances as Shaik Asmeel Shariff vs Mohammad Smaiulla Khan on 5 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/187410965/

sentences.text:
As such, considering the entire materials on record, I am of the opinion that the accused has failed to rebut the presumptions available in favour of the complainant and the complainant has successfully established his case beyond all reasonable doubts and hence, the accused is to be held guilty for the commission of the offence punishable under Sec.138 of Negotiable Instruments Act.
14.

It is relevant to mention here that the accused having issued cheque in favour of the complainant, the accused has failed to pay the cheque amount and hence, the complainant is to be suitably compensated for the delay caused by the accused in its repayment.

Further the punishment prescribed for the offence U/s.138 of Negotiable Instruments Act is imprisonment for a period which may extend to two years or with C.C.NO.52035/2023 fine which may extend to twice the amount of the cheque or with both.

Considering the facts and circumstances of this case, nature,
year of the transaction, nature of the instrument involved, cost of litigation and the rate of interest proposed by Hon'ble Supreme Court in 2012 (1) SCC 260 (R.Vijayan Vs Baby), I am of the opinion that it is just and desirable to impose fine of Rs.20,80,000/- and out of the said amount, it seems to be proper to award a sum of Rs.20,70,000/- as compensation to the complainant as provided U/s.357(1) of Cr.P.C and the remaining sum of Rs.10,000/- shall go to the State towards expenses.
With these observations, my findings on Point No.1 is in the Affirmative.

In default, the accused shall undergo simple imprisonment for 6 months.

shall be paid to the State towards expenses and remaining amount of Rs.20,70,000/- to the complainant as compensation as per the provisions of Sec.357(1) of Cr.P.C.

opennyai_summary.facts:
The complainant has filed this private complaint under Section.200 of Cr.P.C., against the accused for the offence punishable U/s. 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act.
Thereafter, on various occasions, the accused requested for the amounts towards clearing pending taxes, transfer of katha, addressing additional issues at Bank, paying certain dues to his brother etc., all issues concerned to the property belonging to him and hence, the complainant ended up paying Rs.30,000/-
on 29.10.2018, Rs.10,000/- on 30.10.2018, Rs.2,000/- on 28.12.2018, Rs.2,00,000/-
on 01.02.2019 and Rs.1,00,000/- on 01.02.2018.
The moment the bounced cheque was kept on the table, where the accused was writing the fresh cheque, the accused took hold of the bounced cheque and started to run out of the house.
The accused started threatening the complainant and his family of death and rode away on his bike.
The accused has illegally taken possession of the bounced cheque.
The accused after avoiding the police for more than a week has finally come to the police station and given a statement giving vague reasons and a concocted story, which is totally not believable.
After learning from the jurisdictional police station that they would treat the NCR No.29/2020 as closed after obtaining a statement from the accused person and that the complainant could approach the court for relief, the complainant has approached the jurisdictional court on 01.02.2020 with a private complaint against the accused person for offences under sections 420, 506 of the Indian Penal Code.
The complainant got issued legal notice to the accused on 04.02.2020 calling upon the accused for repayment of the cheque amount.
The notice sent to the accused was duly received by the accused on C.C.NO.52035/2023 05.02.2020.
Inspite of receipt of notice, the accused failed to pay the cheque amount, but the accused has caused a reply to the said notice on 15.02.2020 stating false averments and a fabricated story.
Hence, the accused has committed the offence punishable U/s.138 of Negotiable Instruments Act.
3. Based on the complaint, the sworn statement affidavit, the documents, etc., the court took cognizance of an offence punishable under Sec.138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act by following the guidelines of Apex Court issued in Indian Bank Association's case and ordered to register a criminal case against the accused for the offence punishable U/ s.138 of Negotiable Instruments Act.
opennyai_summary.issue:

1. Whether the complainant proves beyond all reasonable doubts that the accused has committed an o/p/u/s 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act?
2. What Order?

5 7.
It is C.C.NO.52035/2023 relevant to mention here that the accused is not disputing the fact that Ex.P14 pertains to his account and he is also not disputing the fact that the signature on the said cheque in question belongs to him.
Once the presumption U/S 139 and 118 of the Negotiable Instruments Act is raised, it is for the accused to rebut the said presumptions by adducing cogent evidence in support of his defence.
It is relevant to mention here that even though the accused has issued the reply notice after the lodging of said police complaint and dishonor of the said cheque in question as could be ascertained from the date of said documents, the accused did not take any legal action against the complainant either for misuse of the security cheque or for lodging false complaint or for recovery of the said money of Rs.16,00,000/- and Rs.25,00,000/- till this date.
Further it is relevant to mention here that the accused though stated that the said advance C.C.NO.52035/2023 money of Rs.10,00,000/- towards the construction of shed was paid by the complainant to his bank account maintained in Bank of India, the accused did not produce his bank Shaik Asmeel Shariff vs Mohammad Smaiulla Khan on 5 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/187410965/
7 statement reflecting such entry for the best reasons known to him.
Further the complainant has done and taken all the necessary actions against the accused as a prudent man would have been done in the above said facts and circumstances as Shaik Asmeel Shariff vs Mohammad Smaiulla Khan on 5 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/187410965/
8 could be seen from the materials on record.
As such, considering the entire materials on record, I am of the opinion that the accused has failed to rebut the presumptions available in favour of the complainant and the complainant has successfully established his case beyond all reasonable doubts and hence, the accused is to be held guilty for the commission of the offence punishable under Sec.138 of Negotiable Instruments Act.
14.
Further the punishment prescribed for the offence U/s.138 of Negotiable Instruments Act is imprisonment for a period which may extend to two years or with C.C.NO.52035/2023 fine which may extend to twice the amount of the cheque or with both.
Considering the facts and circumstances of this case, nature,
year of the transaction, nature of the instrument involved, cost of litigation and the rate of interest proposed by Hon'ble Supreme Court in 2012 (1) SCC 260 (R.Vijayan Vs Baby), I am of the opinion that it is just and desirable to impose fine of Rs.20,80,000/- and out of the said amount, it seems to be proper to award a sum of Rs.20,70,000/- as compensation to the complainant as provided U/s.357(1) of Cr.P.C and the remaining sum of Rs.10,000/- shall go to the State towards expenses.
opennyai_summary.arguments:
Such being the case, once the accused accepts and admits that the cheque in question pertains to the account of the accused and that the signature on the cheque in question pertains to him, the initial presumption as contemplated U/S 139 of the N.I Act has to be raised by the court in favour of the complainant, however, the accused is entitled to rebut the said presumption as held in the case of Sri Rangappa Vs. Sri Mohan by the Hon'ble Supreme Court reported in AIR 2010 SC 1898.

the accused recovered C.C.NO.52035/2023 for the complainant the said land by incurring all the expenses for himself and when it was restored in favour of the complainant, the complainant failed to give the accused said 2 guntas of land as assured and after discussion, the complainant had agreed to give Rs.25,00,000/- and he did not pay even the said amount to the accused and that the complainant has filed false complaint against the accused and that the complainant is liable to pay to the accused the remaining amount of Rs.16,00,000/- towards the construction work carried out by the accused and amount of Rs.25,00,000/- towards the cost incurred by the accused in restoring the above said 6 guntas of land in favour of the complainant.
